EDUCATIONAL_OBJECTIVE: Patients with depression can be mistakenly labeled as treatment-resistant if they fail to receive an adequate antidepressant trial. Antidepressants should be continued for at least 6 weeks at a therapeutic dosage before considering medication augmentation or switching. EXPLANATION: adequate antidepressant trial is generally considered to be 6 weeks at a therapeutic dosage. Patients may be mistakenly labeled as treatment-resistant if they do not receive an adequate antidepressant trial. This patient has taken sertraline 100 mg for only 2 weeks and is beginning to show signs of response (eg, improvement in sleep and appetite). The physician should explain that 2 weeks at the 100-mg dosage is an inadequate trial and recommend that the patient continue sertraline for an additional 4 weeks. The initial 2-week period when the patient was on a subtherapeutic dose of 25 mg should not be counted as part of the trial. Physicians should be aware that inadequate dosage and/or duration is a common reason for perceived inefficacy. Patients may become easily discouraged, leading to nonadherence or premature medication changes and/or inappropriate polypharmacy on the part of the physician. To achieve a positive outcome, it is essential to explain the typical time course of antidepressant response and to encourage the patient to complete an adequate trial. (Choice A) Patients should receive an adequate trial of monotherapy before considering augmentation with a second medication. (Choices C and D) It would be premature to discontinue sertraline 100 mg after 2 weeks. Switching to an alternate antidepressant such as bupropion or venlafaxine can be considered if the patient has minimal response to a maximally tolerated dosage after 6 weeks. (Choice E) Increasing the dosage would not be indicated at this point as the patient is showing signs of responding to sertraline 100 mg. The dose should be maintained for the duration of an adequate trial. Increasing the dosage prematurely risks exposing the patient to unnecessary side effects. Patients usually present with antibiotic-nonresponsive pneumonia 4-12 weeks after neck or thoracic radiation treatment. Fever, dyspnea, cough, and pleuritic chest pain are common, as is leukocytosis. Treatment for ARP includes prednisone for 2 weeks with a gradual taper over 3-12 weeks; however, this is unlikely to benefit established fibrotic disease. (Choice A) Doxycycline is indicated for atypical bacterial pneumonia; however, moxifloxacin provides atypical coverage. Failure to improve on moxifloxacin makes atypical bacterial pneumonia unlikely. (Choice B) Furosemide would treat volume overload due to heart failure; however, bibasilar crackles would be expected and pleuritic chest pain would be unusual. (Choice D) Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treats Pneumocystis pneumonia, which usually presents with diffuse, bilateral interstitial or alveolar infiltrates in patients who are immunosuppressed. The diagnosis is unlikely in this patient with no known impairment in cell-mediated immunity (eg, HIV). (Choice E) Fungal infections with endemic (eg, histoplasmosis) or opportunistic (eg, aspergillosis) organisms can mimic bacterial pneumonia. However, endemic fungi are not typically treated with voriconazole; pulmonary aspergillosis classically manifests with nodular opacities, sometimes with cavitation (chronic necrotizing aspergillosis), and affected patients are typically neutropenic (invasive aspergillosis). ARP is a more likely diagnosis in this patient who has not received chemotherapy, has a relatively nontoxic presentation, and recently underwent radiation therapy. In addition, she has renal insufficiency and alkalosis. Together, this triad is most consistent with milk-alkali syndrome (MAS). MAS is caused by excessive intake of calcium and absorbable alkali, most commonly due to the use of calcium carbonate preparations for osteoporosis or heartburn. The resulting hypercalcemia causes renal vasoconstriction with decreased glomerular blood flow and leads to increased natriuresis, with eventual volume depletion and metabolic alkalosis due to increased renal tubular bicarbonate resorption. Manifestations can range from incidental hypercalcemia, to acute symptomatic hypercalcemia, to chronic kidney disease with metastatic calcification. The hypercalcemia in MAS corrects promptly with isotonic saline infusion and (if necessary) furosemide. This patient's 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D level is at the low end of normal. (Choice B) Malignancy-induced hypercalcemia is possible in this patient but less likely than MAS in light of her history of taking an over-the-counter medication for heartburn (most likely calcium carbonate), coexistent alkalosis, and rapid correction with normal saline. (Choice D) This patient has a suppressed PTH level, which rules out primary hyperparathyroidism. (Choice E) Thiazide diuretics can cause hypercalcemia due to increased renal reabsorption of calcium. Although thiazides can increase the risk for MAS, the hypercalcemia attributable to thiazides is usually very mild and rarely symptomatic. TAKEAWAY: ⭐ PERSONAL TAKEAWAY: h severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, jaundice, ascit EDUCATIONAL_OBJECTIVE: Budd-Chiari syndrome (thrombosis of hepatic veins) should be suspected in young women who present with rapid onset of abdominal pain and ascites. Diagnosis is made by ultrasound with Doppler flow, computed tomography scan, or magnetic resonance angiography. Treatment includes anticoagulation, treatment of liver complications, angioplasty, transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunts, or liver transplant. EXPLANATION: This patient's clinical presentation suggests Budd-Chiari syndrome. Budd-Chiari syndrome is due to thrombosis of the hepatic/intrahepatic veins or suprahepatic inferior vena cava and occurs most commonly in women in their 30s and 40s. The condition may be idiopathic or due to etiologies such as malignancy (eg, hepatocellular carcinoma is most common), myeloproliferative diseases, oral contraceptive use, pregnancy, or hypercoagulable states. Acute Budd-Chiari syndrome (20% of patients) presents with severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, jaundice, ascites, and possible variceal bleeding. Serum aminotransferases are usually elevated, but not as high as in acute viral hepatitis (Choice B). Untreated disease may progress to encephalopathy and fulminant liver failure. Subacute and chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome may be asymptomatic for weeks to several months due to partial hepatic vein occlusion. Chronic hepatic vein occlusion may lead to hypertrophy of the caudate lobe of the liver, which eventually compresses the infrahepatic inferior vena cava to cause ascites and lower-extremity edema. Patients eventually develop cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and normal to mildly elevated liver function studies. However, jaundice and encephalopathy are less common. Diagnosis can be made by Doppler ultrasound with flow, CT scan, or magnetic resonance angiography showing occlusion or poorly visualized flow in the hepatic veins. Venography (gold standard) is suggested if these tests are nondiagnostic and may show venous occlusion with a "spider-web" pattern of hepatic collaterals. Ascites fluid analysis usually shows a high serum to ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) > 1.1 g/dL, indicating portal hypertension. Liver biopsy is reserved for patients with inconclusive initial investigations. Treatment involves diuretics, anticoagulation, angioplasty with stenting for select patients, and possible thrombolytics (only in acute/subacute disease). Patients not responding to these measures may require transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt, surgical shunts, or liver transplant. cards.explanation: This patient's clinical presentation suggests Budd-Chiari syndrome. Budd-Chiari syndrome is due to thrombosis of the hepatic/intrahepatic veins or suprahepatic inferior vena cava and occurs most commonly in women in their 30s and 40s. Serum aminotransferases are usually elevated, but not as high as in acute viral hepatitis (Choice B). Untreated disease may progress to encephalopathy and fulminant liver failure. Subacute and chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome may be asymptomatic for weeks to several months due to partial hepatic vein occlusion. TAKEAWAY: ⭐ PERSONAL TAKEAWAY: hyperintense T2/FLAIR signal HTN PRES EDUCATIONAL_OBJECTIVE: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) is a condition with broad clinical symptoms. It presents with acute to subacute onset of severe headache (thunderclap), hemiparesis, seizures, altered mentation, and visual impairment. A brain MRI commonly shows evidence of symmetrical hyperintense T2/FLAIR signal abnormalities predominantly in the subcortical white matter of posterior parieto-occipital lobes suggestive of vasogenic edema. Hypertensive crisis is one of the many causes of PRES, which is believed to be the result of impaired cerebral autoregulation. EXPLANATION: often seen in the setting of hypertensive crises (hypertensive encephalopathy), chemotherapeutic agents (e.g., cyclosporine), eclampsia/preeclampsia, allogenic bone marrow transplantation, medical renal disease, autoimmune disease, sepsis, and shock. TABLE Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) Synonymous names Reversible posterior cerebral edema Posterior leukoencephalopathy syndrome Hyperperfusion encephalopathy Brain capillary leak syndrome Clinical features Headaches (thunderclap) not responsive to analgesics Altered mentation (can range from confusion to coma) Visual disturbances (e.g., hallucinations, cortical blindness) Seizures (usually generalized tonic-clonic) Hemiparesis Neuroimaging Brain MRI with symmetrical hyperintense T2/FLAIR signal abnormalities in subcortical posterior parieto-occipital white matter Cerebellum and brainstem can also be involved PRES is due to brain edema, possibly as a result of diminished sympathetic innervation of the posterior circulation. The posterior regions of the brain are more susceptible to injury from high mean arterial pressures, which lead to increased fluid migration into the brain parenchyma and subsequent vasogenic edema. It may also occur from cerebrovascular endothelial injury (vasculopathy). The parietal and occipital lobes are most commonly affected, followed by the frontal lobes, inferior temporal-occipital junction, and cerebellum. There have been rare case reports of PRES affecting the brainstem and the cervical cord as well. Diffusion weighted MRI studies of the brain are usually normal in the setting of PRES, and therefore confirm that the abnormalities seen in the cortical and subcortical white matter represent reversible vasogenic edema. Treatment includes lowering blood pressure and antiepileptic therapy for seizures, with most patients experiencing reversal of their symptoms within 2 weeks.
